I did not find a study combining all requested controls for jointly trained item-ID/text sequential recommenders with no pretrained encoder. The closest recommendation precedent is Harte et al., *Leveraging Large Language Models for Sequential Recommendation* (RecSys 2023): permuting pretrained embeddings across items substantially degraded LLM2BERT4Rec, below vanilla BERT4Rec. Their analysis also identifies brand relationships in Amazon Beauty. This supports testing item–text alignment, but does not isolate attribute semantics from brand cues or establish the result for text encoders trained from scratch. [Authors’ supplementary analysis](https://github.com/dh-r/LLM-Sequential-Recommendation/blob/main/online_material.md).

Word-order research supplies useful methodological cautions. *Out of Order* finds that many BERT predictions survive word shuffling; *Word Order Does Matter* shows shuffled-training controls can retain order information through subword segmentation and correlations between sentence length and unigram probabilities. Thus, shuffling is not a clean semantic null, and sensitivity alone does not demonstrate understanding. *NumPert* provides an adjacent precedent for controlled numerical changes, including label-flipping probes, although it evaluates fact-checking rather than recommendation. [Out of Order](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.15180), [Word Order Does Matter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.10995), [NumPert](https://aclanthology.org/2025.ijcnlp-srw.8/).

The defensible opportunity is the combined evaluation protocol: retrain separately with fixed item–text permutations within popularity, text-length and availability strata; compare intact text, brand-masked text and shuffled tokens; pair meaning-preserving rewrites with meaningful numerical-attribute changes. Measure validation ranking accuracy alongside perturbation sensitivity. These are proposed adaptations, not a verified established protocol. Matching and retraining would strengthen the evidence beyond inference-only corruption, but this search does not establish a first-of-kind novelty claim.
